figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Primary amide N-methyltransferase in ansacarbamitocin biosynthesis. (A) Representative chemical structures of ansacarbamitocins,
maytansine and ansamitocins. (B) Reassembled asc cluster encoded ansacarbamitocin biosynthesis and the asm cluster responsible for ansamitocin
biosynthesis. (C) Phylogenetic analysis of Asc-Orf2 with the reported amide N-methyltransferases. Details of these enzymes were listed in Table
S4.4,5,13−20

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Functional characterization of Asc-Orf2. (A) Metabolic profiles of A. alba DSM 44262 and the Δasc-orf2 mutant. Compounds 1 and 2
differ by the presence of the 4,5-epoxide or 4,5-double bond, while 3 and 4 differ by the presence or absence of a methyl group at the 3′−OH of the
glycosyl moiety. (B) Enzymatic assays of Asc-Orf2 with diverse substrates using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. Compounds 5,
7, and 9 were isolated the A. pretiosum mutant strain that overexpressed the asc21b gene in our previous studies, while the methylated product 6
was originally isolated from A. alba 44262Δasc25.10,11 (C) Kinetic parameters of Asc-Orf2 with substrate 5.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Structure and catalytic mechanism of Asc-Orf2. (A) X-ray crystal structure of Asc-Orf2 in complexed with SAH (PDB: 9L4Q). Omit
electron density map (2Fo-Fc) of SAH was contoured at the 1σ level. (B) Molecular docking analysis of SAM and 5 binding to Asc-Orf2. Key
catalytic residues and binding-related residues were highlighted in goldenrod. (C) Sequence alignment of Asc-Orf2 with the representative
PF05175 family enzymes, highlighting its unique 116NPPH119 catalytic motif (Table S6). (D) Comparison of enzymatic activity of Asc-Orf2 and key
active-site variants. The conversion of 5 to 6 by the wild-type (WT) enzyme was set to 100%. N.D. indicated no detectable activity. (E) Michaelis−
Menten kinetics of Asc-Orf2 mutants N116D and N116A, respectively. N116D (Km: 16 ± 2 μM, kcat: 2.04 ± 0.08 min−1, kcat/Km: 0.13 μM−1·
min−1); N116A (Km: 24 ± 3 μM, kcat: 0.84 ± 0.05 min−1, kcat/Km: 0.035 μM−1·min−1). R2 values for the fitting curves were 0.9813 and 0.9761,
respectively. (F) The proposed mechanism of Asc-Orf2-catalyzed 3-O-carbamoyl N-methylation via its unique NPPH motif.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Combinatorial biosynthesis of 3-O-(N-methyl)-carbamoyl derivatives of maytansinol. (A) Metabolic profiles of HGF052 mutant strains
overexpressing the asc21b and asc-orf2 genes. HGF052 refers to the A. pretiosum ATCC 31565Δasm19 strain.24 Compound 8 was obtained via in
vitro enzymatic conversion from 7 (Figure 2B). (B) The proposed post-PKS modification pathways for the derivatives, with the enzymes colored
corresponding to their respective modification sites in the chemical structures.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Functional expansion of Asc-Orf2. (A) Molecular docking analysis of 8 with β-tubulin, with hydrogen bonds indicated in yellow. (B)
Catalytic conversion of 7 to 13 using allyl analog of SAM, namely, S-adenosyl (S)-2-amino-4-(allylthio)butanoic acid (SAAll) as an alkyl donor.
(C) Structural analysis of Asc-Orf2 focusing on key residues surrounding the alkyl donor. (D) Characterization of the activity of Asc-Orf2 and its
mutant Asc-Orf2V141G toward SAAll, with corresponding ESI mass spectrometric detection of 13.
